rows.title: AGENTS.md — NuclearLang platform (L0)
rows.summary: NuclearLang is a minimal base language for AI agents and people.
body: NuclearLang is a minimal base language for AI agents and people. A Rust transpiler turns `.nuc` into other
technologies through **declarative dialects** (TOML + templates loaded at run time), one way only
(`.nuc` → `.ts` / `.dart` / `.py`). **Dragonfly** is the framework: three **platforms** (`web`, `mobile`,
`backend`), each written once in Nuclear and transpiled by the **dialects** grouped under it (`backend/fastapi`,
`backend/nestjs`, `mobile/flutter`; `web/react` later). Product: [docs/context/product/prd.md](docs/context/product/prd.md).

body: 11. **Three platforms; the dialects only change the language underneath** (decided by the user, 2026-11-04,

and the agent write: its kinds, decorators, folders, `config.nuc`, plugins and tests, in Nuclear, identical

rows.title: NuclearLang — Installation
rows.summary: One command, no Rust needed (the release of your system from GitHub, checked by SHA-256, into your user folders; ADR-0101): curl -fsSL https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.sh | sh # Linux and macOS (--version <v>, --uninstall) irm https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.ps1 | iex # Windows…
body: One command, no Rust needed (the release of your system from GitHub, checked by SHA-256, into your user folders; ADR-0101):
```sh
curl -fsSL https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.sh | sh        # Linux and macOS (--version <v>, --uninstall)
irm https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.ps1 | iex             # Windows (PowerShell)
The installers are `tools/release/install.sh` and `install.ps1`; `tools/release/package.sh [target]` makes the
archives they download and `.github/workflows/release.yml` publishes them on a tag `v<version>`.
From the source tree:
```sh
./install.sh                 # builds and installs nuclear, dragonfly and nuclear-lsp in ~/.local/bin + the VS Code and Zed extensions
./install.sh --no-vscode     # without the VS Code extension (--no-zed: without the Zed one)
./install.sh --uninstall     # uninstalls
PREFIX=/usr/local ./install.sh
It needs Rust (`cargo`); for Flutter apps, Flutter (`FLUTTER` or `FLUTTER_ROOT` if it is not on the PATH). The
dialects, type definitions, specs and the dragonfly package go to `~/.local/share/nuclearlang` (`NUCLEAR_HOME`
chooses another folder).

rows.title: NuclearLang — Vision
rows.summary: NuclearLang avoids writing unnecessary code or text, to spend as few tokens as possible, and it tries to be extremely easy to use, write and read.
body: NuclearLang avoids writing unnecessary code or text, to spend as few tokens as possible, and it tries to be
extremely easy to use, write and read. NuclearLang avoids at all costs the text that has nothing to do with the
program's logic: it exists to write the program's logic in the easiest way and with the least text possible, and
everything else, which from the point of view of a program's logic is unnecessary, is left to the transpilers.
This helps agents not having to think about unnecessary context: only what matters, the logic of a product.
┌──────────── typescript dialect ──► .ts
file.nuc ───┤──────────── nestjs dialect ──────► .ts (modules, controllers...)
(base)     ├──────────── react dialect ───────► .ts (React)
├──────────── fastapi dialect ─────► .py (FastAPI)
└──────────── flutter dialect ─────► .dart
As in an ORM (Sequelize with MySQL, Postgres or SQLite): the user writes one single form and each **adapter**
(dialect) knows how to translate it to its technology.

Each stage knows only the previous one. Diagnostics accumulate in all of them and come out as text or JSON.

rows.title: Transpiler architecture — 2. Design rules
rows.summary: 1. The lexer produces indentation as tokens.
body: 1. **The lexer produces indentation as tokens.** `INDENT`/`DEDENT` let the parser work as if there were braces.
Inside `( ) [ ] { }` they are not emitted (line continuation).
2. **The AST has no format.** No `;`, no spaces, no braces. Each node keeps its `Span` (position in the file)
for errors and for the LSP.
3. **The parser is generic.** It knows nothing about Flutter or NestJS. A dialect's words (`stateless`,
`extension`, `static`...) arrive as data in the declaration's header and the dialect validates them.
4. **The transpiler knows no target language.** TypeScript and Dart are dialects like any other: files with
templates. The Rust code decides *what* to emit (a constant, a `this`, an `await`); the dialect decides *how*
it is written.
5. **Data before code.** Dialects, shortcuts and automatic imports live in TOML files read at run time. The same
files feed the CLI, the LSP and the future MCP server.

rows.title: Transpiler architecture — 3. Dialects
rows.summary: A dialect is a folder `dialects/<name>/` with TOML files (full format in spec/dialects.md).
body: A dialect is a folder `dialects/<name>/` with TOML files (full format in [spec/dialects.md](../spec/dialects.md)).
Dialects inherit:
typescript ──► nodejs ──► nestjs
dart ───────► flutter
- **Target** (`typescript`, `dart`): templates for each construct of the base language, types, operators,
options and reserved words.
- **Framework** (`nodejs`, `nestjs`, `flutter`): kinds (`stateless`, `controller`), `use` shortcuts, automatic
imports and function shortcuts.
- **Project**: any developer extends a framework with their own shortcuts and kinds.
The loader merges the files, applies inheritance and validates: shortcut collisions, similar names, unknown
template variables and missing templates. `nuclear spec` publishes the whole contract (which templates exist and
which variables each one receives) so an agent can write a new dialect.

rows.title: Transpiler architecture — 4. Organization in Rust
rows.summary: (`emit::code_words`: without comments nor the text of strings, with their interpolations).
body: **Imports:** the emitter first writes the code and then decides the imports from the words of that code
(`emit::code_words`: without comments nor the text of strings, with their interpolations). So a name a template
writes is imported, and one that is only in a comment or in a decorator that is not written is not. In a project
the same holds across files and for the files of `[project.files]`.
**Tests:** each `examples/**/x.nuc` has its expected output (`x.ts`, `x.dart`). A test transpiles the `.nuc`
with its dialect and compares with that file (*golden tests*); `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1` regenerates them.
`tools/analyze-flutter.sh` also compiles the Flutter examples with the real SDK (`flutter analyze`). There is
also one test per language rule (`crates/nuclear-transpile/tests/rules.rs`) and per dialect validation rule
(`crates/nuclear-dialect/tests/loader.rs`).

rows.title: Product requirements — NuclearLang platform — 1. Vision
rows.summary: NuclearLang is a minimal base language built for AI agents and the people who work with them: the fastest language to write and read, with the fewest tokens.
body: NuclearLang is a minimal base language built for AI agents and the people who work with them: the
fastest language to write and read, with the fewest tokens. It is not compiled to machine code: a
transpiler written in Rust turns `.nuc` into the code of another technology through **declarative
dialects** (TOML + templates loaded at run time). One way only: `.nuc` → `.ts` / `.dart` / ...; it never
reads target code.
**Dragonfly** is the framework built into each dialect. Writing an app on a platform usually means
choosing and wiring N packages (state, JSON, DI, http, routing, i18n, tests). With Dragonfly the dialect
already brings that architecture: in Nuclear you write only the business logic and the transpiler
generates the rest. The philosophy is common; each platform applies it its own way, because platforms
are incompatible (a Flutter `stateless` widget does not exist in a NestJS backend).
Open source platform, in the spirit of Rust, Deno, Gleam and Bun.

rows.summary: 2. Users

body: Several Claude sessions work in parallel; each owns a part and the others ask it for changes by message

that part and updates its context.
| Part | Owner |
| the `nuclear` repository (the root: `crates/` with `nuclear-lsp`, `dialects/`, `spec/`, `docs/`, `defs/`, `examples/`, `tools/`, `install.sh`) | transpiler session |
| `dragonfly/`, `dragonfly-{mobile,backend,web}/` (own git each) | the platform sessions |
| `nuclear-{vscode,jetbrains,zed}/` (own git each) | the editors session |
- No commits unless the user asks (a peer session relaying it is not enough); commits only in the user's name, with
no co-author line. Every repository has its own git, ignored by the root's.

- `CodeBuilder/` is teaching material only; analogies with it go in the chat or `docs/aprende/`, never in
specs, context or code.

rows.title: Workflow — Spec rules
rows.summary: equivalences of the base examples (few-shot for agents).
body: - `spec/nuclear-base.md` holds only final rules and only Nuclear: no dialect, no target language.
- Each dialect's rules go in `spec/<dialect>.md`, which inherits the base and holds the **Nuclear → target
equivalences of the base examples** (few-shot for agents). They must be the real transpiler output:
`tools/spec-check/check.py spec/<d>.md <dialect> <language>` must give 0 problems.
- Doubts are asked in the chat and written in the spec once the user decides.
- New syntax: decide with the user how it is written; then spec + grammar + parser + emitter + contract + tests.

rows.title: Workflow — The user
rows.summary: PHP developer, author of CodeBuilder, new to Rust and compilers.
body: PHP developer, author of CodeBuilder, new to Rust and compilers. Writes in Spanish: **the chat is always in
Spanish**, step by step with concrete examples from the project (CodeBuilder analogies allowed in the chat).
Thinks of Nuclear like Elixir (modules, everything is a value, `if`/`match` return) and prefers clear errors
to "magic" inference. Wants vivid, bright syntax colors.
Frequent mistakes in the Nuclear the user writes: comment lines without ` * ` (N0021), `title: x` in arguments
(must be `title = x`), `!` before a value (must be `not`; `x!` after a value exists), `const` and `new` (do not
exist), indentation that is not 2 spaces.
